prose.summary: Welders join and repair metal components to a specified process and acceptance standard. The job combines preparation, blueprint reading, equipment control and inspection. It is not simply making a bead that looks clean.
prose.day_to_day: The work includes identifying materials, preparing joints, setting equipment, welding and checking completed work. Current descriptions include arc, MIG, TIG and shielded-electrode processes on industrial and naval components. Welders also review procedures, tests and documentation where strength, tightness or nondestructive inspection standards apply.
prose.work_environment: This is site-based physical work in fabrication shops, plants, construction settings and repair facilities. Heat, fumes, confined access and protective equipment are normal constraints. Schedules vary with production, installation and shutdown work.
prose.getting_in: Learn safe preparation and one process under supervised practice, then build evidence through welds tested to the target code or employer standard. Blueprint reading and material identification matter alongside hand skill. The license sheet notes AWS code certifications for structural work, while requirements vary by process and employer.
prose.ladder: Early welders handle prepared joints and defined processes under inspection. Responsibility grows toward difficult positions, specialized alloys, procedure qualification, inspection support and technical direction. Adjacent routes include fabrication, maintenance and robotics-technician work.
prose.suits: This work fits people who want physical precision and can repeat a controlled process despite uncomfortable conditions. It requires respect for preparation, safety and inspection. It is a poor fit if appearance matters more than the acceptance test.
prose.misconceptions: Welding is not freehand metal joining where experience replaces procedure. Material, filler, joint preparation, process settings and inspection determine whether the result is acceptable.
prose.who_qualifies: Fabricators, maintenance technicians and people with blueprint or metalworking experience bring adjacent foundations. They still need process-specific practice and tested weld evidence. General tool confidence does not replace qualification to the applicable code.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: Listings cannot show ventilation, fixture quality or whether production pressure encourages skipped preparation. Those shop conditions directly affect safety and weld quality.

steps.how: Practice setup, preparation, travel and shutdown under supervision before chasing several process names.
Interpret joint details, symbols, materials and acceptance requirements before striking an arc.
Use the employer or code acceptance method and treat failure as evidence about preparation or technique.
Pursue the process and code qualification required by the target employer rather than a generic badge.

prose.tools: Welding and fabrication, CAD drafting, blueprint reading, preventive maintenance, hand tools and GD&T appear in the live evidence. MIG, TIG, arc and shielded-electrode processes appear in descriptions. The process specification governs tool choice.

industries.name: Metal fabrication
industries.note: Welders produce assemblies from drawings, fixtures and repeatable procedures.

industries.name: Industrial equipment
industries.note: Work covers pressure, process and machinery components with defined tests.

industries.name: Ship and naval repair
industries.note: Current descriptions include propeller and propulsor manufacturing or repair.

industries.name: Building systems
industries.note: Some openings combine welding with heating or installation work.

specializations.name: Structural welding
specializations.why: It uses code-qualified processes where joint acceptance carries safety consequences.

specializations.name: Pipe and pressure work
specializations.why: It emphasizes tightness, position and controlled procedure.

specializations.name: Repair welding
specializations.why: It works with existing components, uncertain condition and careful material identification.

pros: The work produces a concrete result that can be tested.
Process depth can lead into specialized fabrication and inspection-related work.
cons: The job is physical and exposed to heat, fumes and awkward access.
Certification and qualification requirements vary by process and employer.

faq.q: how do you become a welder?
faq.a: Learn one welding process safely, read drawings and build tested work under supervision. Match later qualifications to the process and code used by target employers.
Sometimes. The license evidence says AWS code certifications are required for structural work, while other jobs use process-specific employer or project qualifications.

faq.q: can welding lead into robotics maintenance?
faq.a: Yes. Fabrication, maintenance and blueprint skills transfer, but PLC, electrical and automation troubleshooting still need to be added.
